text: is pumping the voltage to max and using your figures to overclock safe? I have the rx570 4gb armor
author: @Alvinklauer

text: I don't touch the voltage at all. I do max out the Power Limit but that's not the same thing as voltage. Your graphics card has a power draw limit set on it from the manufacturer which allows it to draw up to a certain amount of power from the wall.  It's kind of a power saving feature. When your card starts working hard playing a game or something and reaches that predetermined limit then it will automatically down clock itself to stay under that limit. Maxing out the Power Limit allows it to draw as much power as your card needs, so essentially you're saying I don't care about power efficiency I want the maximum performance my GPU can do at the current voltage and frequency. So it doesn't add voltage, it just allows the card to suck as much juice as it needs to run at the frequency and voltage you have set. Of course adjusting the frequency does come into play as well. The higher the frequency the faster the card performs but of course there is a limit to just how fast a certain GPU can go, and just because the slider in Afterburner can go higher doesn't mean your GPU can actually go that fast. So getting that dialed in can take a lot of time and trial and error. You can add more voltage to help it achieve a little higher frequency than the stock voltage can achieve but there's only so much voltage a GPU can handle before it burns up. That's why I don't like to mess with the voltage. I'm all about cranking up the Power Limit though, I'd much rather have the performance than the power savings. Anyway, if you have an RX 570 and are using MSI Afterburner you should be able to set the sliders to the same settings I did for this video and get very similar performance. I'm by no means a hardcore overclocker. The overclock I set was based off overclocks I found online that others have fairly easily achieved and I think you should be able to achieve it too. Sorry for the long response but I hope it helps.  Cheers.  :)

author: @OgunZzYT

text: It's the same GPU (the GPU is the actual silicon chip in the graphics card that does all the work) in both cards, the RX 570, so it's capable of the same level of performance.  The difference is in the amount of VRAM.  When running a game all the textures and stuff are loaded into the VRAM.  Some games use more VRAM than others so as long as a game uses less than 4GB of VRAM then the 4GB and 8GB variants will run about the same FPS.  However, once a game begins to use more VRAM than the 4GB (which more and more games these days are beginning to do) then it has to start storing stuff in your system RAM which isn't quite as fast as the GDDR on the graphics card.  This little slow down will result in a lower frame rate.  If you then use up all your system RAM then it has to go to something called the 'page file' which basically means it's streaming if off your hard drive which is WAY slower and results in an even worse frame rate.  Not having enough VRAM is also what is happening when you see textures close to you "popping in." Most games nowadays don't use more than 8GB of VRAM so this means until they start making games use more than 8GB you shouldn't see any performance hit due to a lack of VRAM. That's why I say get the 8GB card.  It's going to be able to keep up better than the 4GB model going forward.
